title: Should and How Often
subtitle: You should rest. You shouldn't share. How often …?
goals: I can name health problems: a cold, a fever, a cough, a sore throat …
I can give advice with should and shouldn’t.
I can ask Should I …? and answer Yes, you should. / No, you shouldn’t.
I can name hygiene habits: brush my teeth, wash my hands …
I can ask How often …? and answer with always, usually, sometimes and never.
I can talk to a doctor and show I care: What’s the matter? I’m sorry.
teacherGoals: Health problems: have a sore throat / a stomachache / a fever / a toothache / an earache / a headache / a cold; cough; sneeze; my (leg) hurts.
Advice: should + base verb (a good idea), shouldn’t + base verb (a bad idea). No -s after should: He should rest (not rests).
Questions: Should I / he …? → Yes, you / he should. / No, you / he shouldn’t.
Hygiene habits: brush my teeth, comb my hair, wash my face, use hand gel, cut my nails, take a shower, wipe my mouth, wash my hands.
Adverbs of frequency before the main verb: always, usually, sometimes, never. How often do / does …? Also every day, once a week.
Talking about problems: What’s the matter? What’s wrong? How are you feeling? Sympathy: I’m sorry. That’s too bad. That’s terrible!
Reading words: germs, clean water, village, well, river, bottle, tap, carry, heavy. Values: honesty, kindness, gratefulness, responsibility.
teacherNote: This week follows Compass Unit 3, pages 44–61: Why do we get sick? Health Problems (46), should / shouldn’t (47), a story about a cold (48–49), the doctor’s advice (50), Talking about Problems (51), writing about a picture (52), a get-well letter and end punctuation (53), Hygiene Habits (54), Adverbs of Frequency (55), clean water (56–57), germs (58), staying on topic (59), values (60) and the unit reflection (61). All sentences and the four short readings are written for this site; only the topics and target words come from the book.

learn.title: Health problems
learn.rule: Say what is wrong: **I have a …** or **My … hurts.**

practice.prompt: Leo holds his tummy. He has a ___.
Ana is very hot. She has a ___.

learn.teacherNote: Pupils act out a problem; the class guesses. Point to the body part: head → headache, tooth → toothache, ear → earache, stomach → stomachache.

learn.title: a or an? -ache words
learn.rule: **have a** headache · **have an** earache. **head + ache = headache.**

examples.label: No -ache word? Say: my leg hurts.

practice.explain: ear starts with a vowel → an.

learn.teacherNote: Show that the -ache words are two small words together. A or an depends on the first sound: an earache.

learn.title: should = a good idea
learn.rule: **should** + verb = **a good idea**. You should rest.

examples.text: You have a cold. You **should** rest.
You have a toothache. You **should** go to the dentist.
You have a fever. You **should** take your temperature.
You are thirsty. You **should** drink water.
You are sneezing. You **should** use a tissue.

practice.prompt: You have a toothache. You should ___.
You have a cold. You should ___.

learn.teacherNote: Should gives advice. Pupils say a problem; a friend gives advice with should. Keep the advice short: You should rest.

learn.title: shouldn’t = a bad idea
learn.rule: **shouldn’t** + verb = **a bad idea**. should + not = shouldn’t.

examples.text: You are sick. You **shouldn’t** share a drink.
examples.label: Germs go from cup to cup.

examples.text: You have a fever. You **shouldn’t** go to school.
You have a toothache. You **shouldn’t** eat lots of candy.

practice.prompt: You have a fever. You ___ go to school.
You have dirty hands. You ___ eat now.

learn.teacherNote: Thumbs up for should, thumbs down for shouldn’t. Read a piece of advice; pupils show the thumb.

learn.title: After should: no -s!
learn.rule: He rest**s** → He should **rest**. After should, the verb never changes.

options: He should go to the doctor.
He should goes to the doctor.

learn.teacherNote: This is the most common mistake: *He should goes*. In Week 1 he → -s. With should, the -s goes away for everybody.

learn.title: Should I …?
learn.rule: Ask for advice: **Should I …?** → **Yes, you should. / No, you shouldn’t.**

examples.q: **Should** I go to school with a fever?

practice.explain: A bad idea → No, he shouldn’t.

learn.teacherNote: Should jumps to the front, like is / are in Week 2. The short answer repeats should: Yes, you should.

learn.title: Problem → advice
learn.rule: Match the problem with the best advice.

examples.a: You should go to the dentist.
You should put on a bandage.
You should take your temperature and rest.
You should go to the school nurse.

options: You should put on a bandage.
practice.explain: A bandage helps a hurt knee.
Cover your mouth when you cough.

learn.teacherNote: Play “Doctor, doctor!”: one pupil says a problem, another gives advice. Swap roles.

learn.title: Hygiene habits
learn.rule: Clean habits keep germs away: **wash my hands, brush my teeth …**
learn.teacherNote: Sing the actions: This is the way I brush my teeth … Pupils mime each habit. Talk about when: in the morning, before lunch, at night.

learn.title: always, usually, sometimes, never

examples.text: Mia **always** brushes her teeth before bed.
examples.label: always = every time

examples.text: Sam **usually** takes a shower in the evening.
examples.label: usually = most times

examples.text: Leo **always** washes his face in the morning.
examples.label: always = every time

examples.text: Mia **usually** wipes her mouth with a napkin.
examples.label: usually = most times

learn.teacherNote: Draw a line from 0% to 100% on the board. Pupils stand at the place that is true for them: I always / usually / sometimes / never …

learn.title: Where does always go?
learn.teacherNote: The adverb sits between who and the verb. The verb keeps its Week 1 form: he always washes.

learn.title: How often …?
learn.rule: **How often do** you …? **How often does** he / she …?

examples.q: **How often do** you brush your teeth?
examples.a: I always brush my teeth after meals.

examples.q: **How often does** Ana use hand gel?
**How often does** Leo cut his nails?
**How often do** they wash their hands?
examples.a: They always wash their hands before meals.

practice.prompt: How often ___ you wash your face?
How often ___ Sam take a shower?

learn.teacherNote: This uses do / does from Week 1. After does the verb has no -s: How often does he wash …?

learn.title: every day, once a week
learn.rule: At the end: **every day · every morning · once a week · twice a day**.

examples.text: Mia brushes her teeth **twice a day**.
examples.label: twice = two times

examples.text: Leo cuts his nails **once a week**.
examples.label: once = one time

examples.q: **How often** do you cut your nails?

practice.explain: In the morning and at night = twice a day.

learn.teacherNote: Phrases with every / once / twice usually go at the end of the sentence, not before the verb.

learn.title: At the doctor’s
learn.rule: Ask: **What’s the matter? What’s wrong?** Be kind: **I’m sorry. That’s too bad.**

examples.text: “I don’t feel well. My throat hurts.”
examples.speaker: Mia

examples.text: “**I’m sorry.** You have a sore throat.”
examples.speaker: Doctor

examples.text: “You should drink warm water and rest.”
examples.speaker: Doctor

examples.text: “**That’s too bad**, Leo. **How are you feeling** now?”
examples.speaker: Ana

practice.prompt: Your friend says: “My leg hurts.” You say:
The doctor asks about the problem:
practice.explain: What’s the matter? = What is the problem?

learn.teacherNote: Role-play: patient says how they feel and what hurts; doctor asks, shows sympathy, names the problem and gives advice.

learn.title: Germs
learn.rule: Germs are **tiny**. They are **everywhere**. Some germs make us **sick**.

examples.text: **Germs** are very small. We can’t see them with our eyes.
Germs are **everywhere**: on doors, desks and pencils.
Germs **spread** when we sneeze and cough.
Sam has **dirty hands**. He should wash them before he eats.
Wash your hands and the germs go away!

practice.prompt: Can we see germs with our eyes?

learn.teacherNote: Put a little glitter on a pupil’s hand and shake hands around the class: the “germs” spread. Then wash hands.

learn.title: First, next, after that, last
learn.rule: A story happens in order: **First … Next … After that … Last …**

examples.text: **First**, Mia wakes up with a cold.
**After that**, she rests in bed and drinks water.
Grandma visits and gives Mia a big **hug**.
examples.label: This happens after that too.

examples.text: Leo and Ana make a **get-well card** for Mia.

learn.teacherNote: Cut a short story into four strips. Pupils put them in order and read them with First, Next, After that, Last.

learn.title: Clean water
learn.rule: Clean water helps us stay **healthy**. Some children walk far to get water.

examples.text: Some children **carry** big, **heavy** bottles from the **river**.
River water is not always clean.
A **well** takes water from deep under the ground.
A **solar panel** gives power to the pump. Clean water comes out of the **tap**.
Now the children can wash their hands with clean water.
examples.label: Clean water stops germs.

practice.prompt: The bottle is full of water. It is ___.
Clean water comes out of the ___.

learn.teacherNote: Talk about where our water comes from. How far do you walk to get water? (Only to the tap!)

learn.title: . ? ! at the end
learn.rule: A sentence ends with **.** A question ends with **?** A strong feeling ends with **!**

examples.text: Dear Sam, I’m sorry you have a cold. You should rest. Get well soon! From Mia
examples.label: A get-well note

learn.teacherNote: Pupils write a short get-well note to a friend: Dear …, I’m sorry …, You should …, Get well soon! From …

learn.title: Values
learn.rule: Values help us decide what to do: **honesty, kindness, gratefulness, responsibility**.

examples.text: Sam feels sick. He tells his mom the truth. That is **honesty**.
Mia makes a card for her sick friend. That is **kindness**.
Mia helps Leo up. Leo says “Thank you!” That is **gratefulness**.
Ana washes the dishes after lunch. That is **responsibility**.
“When I share my crayons, I am being kind.”
examples.speaker: Leo

examples.text: “When I say thank you, I am being grateful.”
examples.speaker: Leo

practice.prompt: You tell the truth. That is ___.

learn.teacherNote: Pupils finish the sentence: When I …, I am being kind / honest / grateful / responsible.

speaking.question: What’s the matter? Act out a health problem.
speaking.sample: I have a headache.

speaking.question: You have a cold. What should you do?
speaking.sample: I should rest and drink water.

speaking.question: You have a toothache. What should you do?
speaking.sample: I should go to the dentist. I shouldn’t eat candy.

speaking.question: Your friend is sneezing. Give some advice.
speaking.sample: You should use a tissue.

speaking.question: What shouldn’t you do when you are sick?
speaking.sample: I shouldn’t share my drink.

speaking.question: Ask for advice. Start with Should I …?
speaking.sample: Should I go to the doctor?

speaking.question: Should you go to school with a fever?
speaking.sample: No, I shouldn’t.

speaking.question: How is your day different when you are sick?
speaking.sample: I stay at home. I don’t go to school.

speaking.question: Name four hygiene habits.
speaking.sample: I wash my hands, brush my teeth, comb my hair and take a shower.

speaking.question: How often do you brush your teeth?
speaking.sample: I always brush my teeth twice a day.

speaking.question: How often do you take a shower?
speaking.sample: I usually take a shower every evening.

speaking.question: What do you never do?
speaking.sample: I never eat with dirty hands.

speaking.question: Which hygiene habit should you do more?
speaking.sample: I should use hand gel more.

speaking.question: When do you wash your hands?
speaking.sample: Before lunch and after the toilet.

speaking.question: You are the doctor. Ask your patient a question.
speaking.sample: What’s the matter? How are you feeling?

speaking.question: Your friend says: “My leg hurts.” Show you care.
speaking.sample: That’s too bad. You should go to the school nurse.

speaking.question: What are germs? Say two things.
speaking.sample: Germs are tiny. They are everywhere.

speaking.question: Name an action that stops germs from spreading.
speaking.sample: We should cover our mouth when we cough.

speaking.question: Why is clean water important?
speaking.sample: Because dirty water can make people sick.

speaking.question: Tell the story of Mia’s cold. Use First, Next, Last.
speaking.sample: First, Mia has a cold. Next, she rests. Last, she feels better.

speaking.question: How can you show kindness to a sick friend?
help: When I …, I am being kind.
speaking.sample: When I make a get-well card, I am being kind.

speaking.question: Why do we get sick? Give your answer.
speaking.sample: Because germs spread. We should wash our hands.
